400.title: The gods choose a human home
400.hook: the gods are offered a cow, then a horse, as a home, and turn both down. then they see a human being
400.carry: the body is a home for the gods
400.tomorrow: hunger and thirst ask for a place
400.howItsDone: In Vedic and later Hindu ritual, the body's senses are linked to deities, and some rites include touching the limbs while reciting mantras, a practice called nyasa, which echoes the idea of the gods dwelling in the body.

segments.voice: Yesterday: atma, the self alone, which looked and said, let me create worlds. The world comes from the one self.
screen: `THE WORLD COMES FROM THE ONE SELF.`

segments.voice: The worlds are made, and the Aitareya has a house-hunting story. The self shapes a cosmic person and draws the great powers out of it: fire, wind, the sun, the moon. Gods. But the gods have nowhere to live. They're adrift, the text says, fallen into a great ocean, and they come back asking for a home. So the self brings them a cow. The gods look it over: no, this isn't enough for us. It brings them a horse. Not enough either. Then it brings them a human being.
screen: `THE GODS HAVE NOWHERE TO LIVE.` → `A COW? NOT ENOUGH.` → `A HORSE? NOT ENOUGH.` → `THEN, A PERSON.`

segments.voice: When the gods see the person, purusha, they say: sukritam bata. Well made, indeed! That's the Upanishad's verdict on the human body. Not a prison. Not a burden. A good piece of work, the house the gods accepted. Then the self says: enter, each into your own place. And no god just walks in. Each one changes shape to fit. Fire becomes speech, and enters the mouth. Wind becomes breath, and enters the nostrils. The sun becomes sight, and enters the eyes. The directions of space become hearing, and enter the ears. Plants and trees become the hairs, and enter the skin. The moon becomes mind, and enters the heart. Death becomes the down-going breath, and enters the navel. The waters become seed, and enter the organ of generation. When you talk, there's fire in your mouth. When you look up, the sun is looking out through you. Your changeable mind is the moon. This is a real thread in Hindu practice: the body as a home for the divine. In some rites a worshipper touches the limbs one by one while saying mantras, a practice called nyasa, placing the sacred in the body. It's saying the great powers out there and the small doors in here belong together, and the person is where they meet. So the next time a mirror or a photo tells you your body is a problem, remember the older verdict. The gods were offered a cow and a horse and said no. They looked at a human being and said: well made, indeed.

segments.voice: Bring attention to your closed mouth, where the story puts fire as speech, then to the breath in the nostrils, the wind, and to the eyes, the sun. Move on to the ears and the directions, the skin and the plants and trees, the heart and the moon as mind. Then rest in the whole house at once, every door open.
The person. Purusha, the human being the gods called well made, the one house where fire, wind, sun and moon could each find their door.
Hold on to this: the body is a home for the gods. Tomorrow, two more guests knock at the door. Four hundred days, done.

401.title: Hunger and thirst get a share
401.hook: once the gods have moved in, two more voices speak up: hunger and thirst want a home too
401.tomorrow: the self enters through the crown of the head
401.howItsDone: Teachers of the Aitareya read this passage when explaining why appetite goes with every sense, and in Vedic ritual each offering is made to a particular deity, the share the passage says hunger and thirst join.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the person, the house the gods called well made, with fire in the mouth and the moon in the heart. Your line was the body is a home for the gods.
screen: `THE BODY IS A HOME FOR THE GODS.`

segments.voice: Everyone's moved in. Fire has the mouth, the sun has the eyes, the moon has the heart. The house is full and humming. Then there's a knock. Two figures stand outside, and they were there before the gods arrived. In fact, they're why the gods went house-hunting at all. Their names are hunger and thirst, ashanaya and pipasa, and they say to the self: what about us? Find us a place too. You know these two: mid-afternoon, midnight at the fridge, long meetings. The Aitareya gives them a whole verse.
screen: `THE HOUSE IS FULL.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `HUNGER AND THIRST: WHAT ABOUT US?`

segments.voice: Here's the order in the story. When the gods first fell into the great ocean, the self touched that whole creation with hunger and thirst. That's why the gods asked for a home: they wanted a place to eat. So hunger and thirst are older than the house. They didn't break in. They were part of the plan. Now, with the gods settled, the two ask: find a place for us. The self doesn't banish them, or scold them as enemies of the spirit. It says, more or less: I'll give you a share among these gods. That's why, the text explains, whenever an offering is made to any god, hunger and thirst share in it. Nobody is shamed for being hungry. One way to hear this story is beside a teaching that runs all through Hindu tradition. Kama, desire, pleasure, love, is counted as one of the four aims of a human life, the purusharthas: dharma, right living; artha, making a living; kama, enjoyment; and moksha, freedom. Wanting isn't treated as the enemy. It gets a seat. But notice where the seat is in the story: inside the offering, beside the gods, not in place of them. The tradition holds kama the same way, inside dharma. Enjoy the meal, the song, the love, and enjoy them rightly. So when a craving shows up, the question isn't how to kill it. It's whether it's sitting at the table, or trying to run the house.
screen: `HUNGER AND THIRST WERE THERE FIRST.` · `A SHARE IN EVERY GOD'S OFFERING.` · `KAMA: ONE OF FOUR AIMS OF LIFE.` · `INSIDE DHARMA, NOT IN PLACE OF IT.` · then, large: `WANTING HAS ITS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Check gently for hunger, thirst, or some other wanting: for your phone, for news, for this to be over. Don't obey it and don't fight it; just find where it lives in the body, the stomach, the throat, the hands. Let it sit there, known and given room, without running the house.

Appetite, the hunger and thirst that ask the self for a place. In the Aitareya, they're given no room of their own, but a share in whatever is offered to every god. Its big sister is kama, desire, one of the four aims of life.
Take this with you: kama, wanting has its place. In this story, even hunger gets a seat at the gods' table. See you tomorrow.

402.title: The self comes in at the crown
402.hook: the house is full of gods, and the self asks a strange question: if all of them do all the work, then who am I?
402.carry: atman: the one who sees through every door
402.howItsDone: Some Hindu men, especially in priestly families, keep a tuft of hair, the shikha, near the crown, and some yoga and meditation teachers direct attention to the crown of the head, which later texts call the brahmarandhra.

segments.voice: Yesterday: appetite, hunger and thirst, given a share in every god's offering. Kama, wanting, has its place.

Here's a company where every department runs perfectly. Speech does the talking. Breath does the breathing. The eyes see, the ears hear, the mind thinks. Then the founder walks through the building with an uncomfortable thought: if they all do everything, what am I for? That's where the Aitareya's first chapter ends. The self has made worlds, a person, a house full of gods and appetites. Now it looks at all that working machinery and asks how it could possibly be there without itself.
screen: `EVERY DEPARTMENT RUNS ITSELF.` → `WHAT AM I FOR?` → `THE SELF ASKS THE SAME.`

segments.voice: The text gives the self two questions. How could this be without me? And: by which way shall I enter? Then comes a list, almost comic. If speaking is done by speech, breathing by breath, seeing by the eye, hearing by the ear, thinking by the mind, then who am I? So the self finds its own door. Not the mouth, the nostrils or the eyes; those were taken. It splits open the seam at the very top of the skull, where the bones meet, and enters there. The text names that door vidriti, the cleft, and calls it the place of joy. Every other god came in through a working opening. The self comes in through a door that does nothing at all. It doesn't speak, see or breathe. It's just the way in. Once inside, the self looks around and sees this very person as Brahman, spread out everywhere. Idam adarsham, it says. I have seen this. Here is one of Hinduism's central teachings: atman, the self. Not the eyes, not the voice, not the mind's chatter, but the one who sees through all of them. Later yoga traditions name a point at the crown, the brahmarandhra, and some readers connect it to this passage. The Aitareya's point is simpler. Your talents and senses are doors. You are the one who came in to see. So on the day one door shuts, a lost voice, a hurt knee, a test that went badly, the self hasn't gone anywhere.
screen: `IF THEY DO EVERYTHING, WHO AM I?` · `THE SELF SPLITS THE SEAM AT THE CROWN.` · `I HAVE SEEN THIS.` · `ATMAN: THE ONE WHO SEES.` · then, large: `VIDRITI.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and let your attention rest on the crown of your head, where the seams of the skull meet: air, warmth, the weight of your hair, or nothing much. This spot isn't talking or watching or breathing, and still something is aware of it. Rest in that awareness, the one that came in by the quiet door.
Vidriti, the cleft at the crown of the head where the self enters. In the Aitareya, after every god has its door, the self comes in through this door, and sees.

403.title: Three births: the third is death
403.hook: the Aitareya counts a person's births, and gets to three, and the third one is what most people would call dying
403.howItsDone: Hindu life-cycle rites, the samskaras, mark stages from before birth through death, and the funeral rites (antyeshti) and later shraddha offerings are understood by many families as sending the departed on to their next life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vidriti, atman: the one who sees through every door of the head, where the self, atman, came in and said, I have seen this.

How many birthdays do you have? One, obviously. It's on your ID. Ask a family and it gets fuzzier. There's the day you were born. There's the day, months before, when someone found out you were coming. And in some families there's a day after the person is gone, when the family gathers and the rites send them on. The Aitareya's second chapter counts births too. It counts three, and it puts them somewhere you might not expect.
screen: `HOW MANY BIRTHDAYS DO YOU HAVE?` → `THE DAY SOMEONE FOUND OUT.` → `THE AITAREYA COUNTS THREE.`

segments.voice: The first birth, the text says, happens in the father. The seed is the strength gathered from all his limbs, a self carried in himself. When he places it in the mother, that's the first birth. Then the second. The child becomes one with the mother, and so, the text says, she doesn't harm it. She nourishes this self inside her, and so she is to be nourished in turn. The father cares for the child before birth and after, and so the line goes on and the worlds continue. The child's arrival is the second birth. Then the third. The child grows and takes the parent's place, carrying on the good work. And the parent, having done what there was to do, grows old and departs. And departing, the text says, he is born again. That's the third birth. Here is a core Hindu teaching in one line: death isn't the opposite of birth. It's the next one. The self goes on, and the tradition surrounds that crossing with care. The funeral rite is called antyeshti, the last offering, and in the days and years after, families make shraddha offerings for those who have gone ahead. Then the chapter turns to a seer, Vamadeva, and quotes his verse from the Rig Veda: while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. A hundred iron fortresses held me down, and like a hawk I broke out. So when a Hindu family says someone has passed on, they mean on.

Then, gently, think of someone who has died; in the Aitareya's count, that was a birth too. Let a breath go to them, wherever they are.

404.title: Prajnanam brahma: consciousness is Brahman
404.hook: the Aitareya ends by asking which one is the self, and answers with two words that became one of the great sayings
404.tomorrow: six students, one year of practice before asking
404.howItsDone: In the Advaita tradition, the four great sayings are taught to students and to those taking monastic vows, and prajnanam brahma is the one associated with the Rig Veda; teachers in other Vedanta schools comment on the same line differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dying is the third birth, in the father, from the mother, and in departing. Dying is the third birth. Today, the Aitareya's last chapter.

Point at yourself. Where did your finger go? Probably the chest, maybe the face. Now ask: is that me, or is that where I keep the thing that's me? It's a children's puzzle, and a very old one. The Aitareya saves it for its last chapter. After the worlds, the gods moving in, hunger and thirst, the door at the crown and the three births, it stops telling stories and asks straight out: who is this one we call the self? And it ends with two words.
screen: `POINT AT YOURSELF.` → `IS THAT ME?` → `WHICH ONE IS THE SELF?`

segments.voice: First the question: is the self the one by which we see? By which we hear, smell, speak, taste? Then the text looks at the heart and mind and lists what they do. Awareness. Perception. Discernment. Intelligence. Wisdom. Insight. Steadiness. Thought. Reflection. Drive. Memory. Intention. Purpose. Life. Desire. Will. All of these, it says, are only names of prajnana. Prajnana means knowing, awareness, consciousness: pra, forth or fully, and jnana, knowing. Then the list widens. This is Brahman. This is Indra, and Prajapati, and all the gods. The five elements, earth, wind, space, water and fire. Every creature, born from an egg, a womb, moisture or a sprout. Horses, cows, people, elephants, whatever breathes, walks, flies or stands still. All of it rests on consciousness. And then: prajnanam brahma. Consciousness is Brahman. Many Hindu teachers in the Advaita tradition count this among four mahavakyas, great sayings, one from each Veda. This is the Rig Veda's. You've already heard the other three this year: tat tvam asi in the Chandogya, and aham brahma asmi and ayam atma brahma in the Brihadaranyaka. Schools read the saying differently. Advaita hears a strict identity: awareness and Brahman are one. Other Vedanta schools hear Brahman as the conscious ground all knowing depends on, while keeping a distinction between the soul and God. Either way, the text points somewhere specific: not at the finger, but at what's aware of it. And on this reading, the same knowing that looks out of your eyes looks out of everyone else's, the friend, the stranger, the person who annoys you.
screen: `WHICH ONE IS THE SELF?` · `ALL THESE ARE NAMES OF PRAJNANA.` · `EVERYTHING RESTS ON CONSCIOUSNESS.` · `ONE OF FOUR GREAT SAYINGS.` · then, large: `CONSCIOUSNESS IS BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Notice seeing, even with your eyes closed, then hearing, then a thought passing, a memory, a small want. Each time, don't follow the thing; notice the knowing of it: seeing, known; sound, known; thought, known. Then, if you'd like, rest in the knowing itself, which doesn't need anything to hold.
Prajnana, knowing, awareness, consciousness. Prajnanam brahma: consciousness is Brahman, the Aitareya's closing word and, in the Advaita tradition, the great saying of the Rig Veda.
Your line: consciousness is Brahman, prajnanam brahma. Tomorrow, six students arrive with questions. Day four hundred four, done.

405.title: Six students wait a year to ask
405.hook: six seekers arrive at a sage's door with their questions ready, and he tells them to wait a year
405.carry: tapas, brahmacharya and faith, then the question
405.howItsDone: In traditional Hindu learning, a student lives with or near the teacher and studies for long periods before being taught the deepest texts; some Vedanta teachers today still ask students to study and practice before taking up the Upanishads.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prajnana. Prajnanam brahma, consciousness is Brahman, consciousness is brahman that closed the Aitareya. Today, a new Upanishad, and six people with questions.

You've finally got a meeting with the expert. You walk in with your list of questions, and before you can open your mouth, they say: come back in a year. The Prashna Upanishad opens with six serious people who come to a great teacher, wood for his fire in their hands, and that is roughly what he tells them. Prashna means question. The whole Upanishad is built from the questions they ask. But first, they have to wait.
screen: `YOUR LIST OF QUESTIONS, READY.` → `COME BACK IN A YEAR.` → `PRASHNA MEANS QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Tradition places the Prashna in the Atharva Veda. It names its six students one by one: Sukesha Bharadvaja. Satyakama Shaibya. Gargya Sauryayani. Kausalya Ashvalayana. Bhargava of Vidarbha. And Kabandhi Katyayana. They were devoted to Brahman, the text says, grounded in it, seeking the highest. And they came to the sage Pippalada, fuel for his fire in hand, sure he could tell them everything. Pippalada says: stay one more year, with tapas, with brahmacharya, and with shraddha. Discipline, a disciplined life of study, and faith. Then ask whatever you like. And then the line that makes this teacher worth listening to: if we know, we'll tell you all of it. If we know. A great sage, six eager students, and he doesn't promise answers. He promises honesty. This is the heart of a relationship Hindus still keep: guru and shishya, teacher and student. The student arrives with fuel in hand, offering to tend the teacher's fire. The teacher asks for readiness before the deepest teaching. It lives on wherever Hindus learn from a guru: Vedanta, Sanskrit, classical music, dance. Think about what the year does. A question asked the day it occurs to you is often a reflex. A question carried through a year of practice has had time to become real. Some answer themselves. The ones still standing are worth a teacher's time. So when a teacher says not yet, it may not be a door closing. It may be the year Pippalada asked for. In the coming days, each student asks one question.
screen: `SIX STUDENTS, FUEL IN HAND.` · `STAY ONE MORE YEAR.` · `IF WE KNOW, WE'LL TELL YOU.` · `GURU AND SHISHYA.` · then, large: `TAPAS, BRAHMACHARYA, SHRADDHA.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle, and when the urge comes to move, check something or get on with the day, notice it and stay: that's a small tapas. One breath, then the next. If a question rises, let it stand at the door, fuel in hand, until later.
Six students. The seekers of the Prashna Upanishad, told by the sage Pippalada to live a year in discipline and faith before asking, and promised only: if we know, we'll tell you.
Take this with you: tapas, brahmacharya and faith, then the question. Tomorrow, the year is up, and the first student steps forward. See you then.

406.title: Matter, breath and the two paths
406.hook: the first student asks where living things come from, and Pippalada answers with a pair: matter and breath, moon and sun
406.carry: the ancestors' path returns; the gods' path doesn't
406.howItsDone: Many Hindus mark the sun's northward turn at Makar Sankranti in mid-January and treat the northern half of the year, uttarayana, as an auspicious time, an idea that echoes the two paths of texts like this one.

segments.voice: Yesterday: six students, told to wait a year before asking: tapas, brahmacharya and faith, then the question. Now the year is up.

The six students have kept the discipline. The first to step forward is Kabandhi Katyayana, with a question as old as asking: sir, from where are these creatures born? Children ask some version of it. Where did I come from? Where did the dog come from, the ants, the trees? A biologist would answer one way, a grandmother another. Pippalada answers with a story, and at its center is a pair, two things that need each other, the way a song needs both silence and sound.
screen: `THE YEAR IS UP.` → `SIR, WHERE DO CREATURES COME FROM?` → `THE ANSWER IS A PAIR.`

segments.voice: Pippalada says: Prajapati, the lord of creatures, wanted offspring. He did tapas, the inner heat you met with Bhrigu, and from that heat he produced a pair: rayi and prana. Rayi means wealth, substance, matter: the stuff that takes form. Prana is breath, life, the energy that moves it. Then the pair shows up everywhere. The sun is prana. The moon is rayi. Matter and life, always in pairs. Then the answer turns to people. The year itself is Prajapati, and it has two paths, a southern and a northern. Those who honor sacrifice and good works, digging wells, giving, keeping the rites, take the southern path, the path of the ancestors, the pitryana, to the world of the moon. And from there they return, to be born again. Those who seek the self through tapas, a disciplined life, faith and knowledge take the northern path, to the sun, which later tradition calls the path of the gods. That, the text says, is the resting place of breath, the immortal, the fearless. From there they do not return. This is an early form of a teaching every Hindu grows up with: karma, the way how you live shapes the next birth, and moksha, freedom from the circle. The Gita names the two paths too. So when a Hindu grandmother says feeding people is good for the next life, she's on the moon's path. And the hope underneath it is the sun's.
screen: `PRAJAPATI'S TAPAS MAKES A PAIR.` · `RAYI IS MATTER; PRANA IS BREATH.` · `GOOD WORKS: THE MOON, AND BACK.` · `TAPAS, FAITH, KNOWLEDGE: THE SUN, NO RETURN.` · then, large: `TWO PATHS.`

segments.voice: Feel the body's weight, the bones and muscle, the pressure where you touch the chair or floor: that's rayi, matter, the moon side. Then feel the breath moving through it, warming and lifting it: that's prana, the sun side. Rest on both at once, the stillness that holds and the motion that lives; neither one is enough alone.
Rayi, wealth and matter, paired with prana, breath. Where do creatures come from? From rayi and prana, the moon and the sun, which Prajapati made as a pair.

Hold on to this: the ancestors' path returns; the gods' path doesn't. That's week fifty-eight: the person, hunger and thirst, the door at the top, three births, the great saying, six students, and matter and breath. Day four hundred six.
